```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.8)
library(MDPL)
```

## What the weights do

Each observational source $k$ gets a weight $\eta_k\in[0,1]$ that
influences its information in the fused estimate: $\eta_k=0$ ignores the
source and $\eta_k=1$ pools it with the trial. The weight selection is
discussed in the relevant paper - they come from fits aimed to estimate
predictive performance on the **trial** data alone.

```{r sim}
sim <- function(n, bias = 0, shift = 0) {
  X <- rnorm(n, 1); U <- rnorm(n)
  A <- rbinom(n, 1, if (bias == 0) 0.5 else plogis(X - 1 + bias * U))
  data.frame(X = X, A = A,
             Y = 0.5 + shift + X + 0.2 * A + 0.1 * A * X + bias * U + rnorm(n))
}
```

The true effect is $\tau(x)=0.2+0.1x$. `bias` is the strength of an
unmeasured confounder $U$ in the observational data; `shift` moves a
source's outcome by a constant, changing the intercept but **not** the
treatment effect.

## Weights respond to confounding

Fit the same trial against sources with increasing `bias`.

```{r sweep}
set.seed(1)
trial <- sim(300)
biases <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2)
eta <- t(sapply(biases, function(b) mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, list(sim(1000, b)), treat = "A")$eta[1, ]))
data.frame(confounding = biases, round(eta, 2))
```

`fit$eta` has one row per source and one column per *trace multiplier*,
the $\lambda$ in the surrogate
$f(\eta) = g'S^{-1}AS^{-1}g + \lambda\,\mathrm{tr}(AS^{-1})$ that the
Taylor method optimises: the first term is the squared bias a source
adds, the second the variance it removes. `t2` ($\lambda=2$,
leave-one-out) is the default everywhere; `t1` ($\lambda=1$) is more
conservative and is available with `trace = "t1"`.

## Several sources, one weight each

With `K` sources you get `K` weights, found jointly.

```{r multi}
set.seed(2)
trial <- sim(300)
obs <- list(clean = sim(1000, 0), mild = sim(1000, 0.5), strong = sim(1000, 2))
fit <- mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, obs, treat = "A")
round(fit$eta, 2)
```

A source's weight depends on what the others contribute. To treat all
sources as one population, `pooled = TRUE` stacks them and gives a
single weight:

```{r pooled}
round(mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, obs, treat = "A", pooled = TRUE)$eta, 2)
```

Pool when the sources are exchangeable (sites of one registry). Use
per-source weights when quality differs, since pooling averages a bad
source's bias into the good one.

## What the weights are scored on

By default the score covers the **whole parameter vector**: a source is
borrowed from to the extent that it agrees with the trial on everything
in the model.

`target` is an optional extension of the Taylor method that scores only
some parameters. `target = "cate"` uses the treatment-effect terms (here
`A` and `A:X`), so nuisance differences such as the intercept are not
penalised; you can also name parameters, e.g. `target = c("A", "A:X")`.
Take an observational data set with the right effect but a constant outcome shift of 1:

```{r target}
set.seed(3)
trial <- sim(300); shifted <- list(shifted = sim(1000, 0, shift = 1))
rbind(`default (all parameters)` = mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, shifted, treat = "A")$eta[1, ],
      `target = "cate"`          = mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, shifted, treat = "A", target = "cate")$eta[1, ])
```

Scored on everything, the shifted source looks biased through its
intercept; scored on the effect parameters it is borrowed from. With a
`target` the score uses the trial's *marginal* information on those
parameters, so the others are integrated out. `target` applies to the
Taylor method only; ELPD and CV score the whole trial likelihood and
warn if you set it.

## Taylor, ELPD proxy and cross-validation

All three methods search from zero borrowing.

- `method = "taylor"` (default) minimises a quadratic surrogate of the
  trial's predictive score from the estimates and information matrices
  alone, so it is nearly instant.
- `method = "elpd"` is an ELPD *proxy*: for each candidate weight it
  draws from the power posterior and scores the trial data by
  (in-sample) WAIC. It is slower.
- `method = "cv"` is the gold standard: refit the trial without each
  fold, fuse with the unchanged source summaries and score on the
  held-out trial rows.

```{r methods}
set.seed(4)
trial <- sim(300); one <- list(mild = sim(1000, 0.5))
system.time(ft <- mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, one, treat = "A"))
system.time(fe <- mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, one, treat = "A", method = "elpd"))
system.time(fc <- mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, one, treat = "A", method = "cv", folds = 5))
rbind(taylor = ft$eta[1, ], elpd = fe$eta[1, ], cv = fc$eta[1, ])
```

The ELPD route also returns its profile; a flat one means the data
barely distinguish heavy from light borrowing.

```{r elpd-plot}
plot(elpd ~ eta, data = fe$selection$table, type = "b", pch = 16,
     xlab = expression(eta), ylab = "ELPD proxy (WAIC) on the trial")
abline(v = fe$eta[1, 1], lty = 2)
```

### Cross-validation options

`folds` is the number of folds, or a vector of fold labels.
`type = "if"` replaces the refits by influence-function leave-one-out
where the model supplies it. The held-out score is the trial's own loss
(minus the log-likelihood) unless you pass `loss`: a function of the
fused parameters, the held-out data and the trial model that returns one
value per row (lower is better).

```{r cv-loss}
my_loss <- function(Theta, data, model) (Theta[, "A"] - 0.2)^2
mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, one, treat = "A", method = "cv", folds = 5,
     loss = my_loss)$eta
```

For `method = "taylor"` the analogue is `metric`, the matrix (or a
function of the trial model returning it) of the quadratic form that
scores the fused estimate; the default is the trial information, and it
overrides `target`.

```{r metric}
H <- diag(c(0, 0, 1, 1))   # score only the last two coefficients
mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, one, treat = "A", metric = H)$eta
```

Use Taylor by default, ELPD for the profile, and CV as a reference check
or for a different loss.
